title: Mesa Colorado Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Mesa wells have a 130 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $12,500-$21,800.
h1: Mesa, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
For rural property around Mesa, the local well records point to moderate drilling depths but variable ground conditions. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 130 feet, while the median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. Most permits are for domestic or household use, and the named geology is usually an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer.

Those numbers help with early budgeting, but they do not guarantee what a particular lot will produce. A driller's bid, pump selection, septic layout, and water-quality testing should be based on the parcel and nearby well records, not only on the area median.

sections.heading: Mesa well depths depend on sediment and fractured bedrock
sections.html:
The 130-foot median is a useful starting point for Mesa, but the spread is wide. The middle half of reported wells runs from 80 to 245 feet. About 34% are under 100 feet, 48% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 16% are between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 733 feet.

Records identify the aquifer as unnamed or fractured bedrock for 667 wells, with only a few permits naming the Mesa Verde Group or Wasatch. In fractured rock, nearby wells can differ substantially. Give a driller the neighboring depths before accepting a fixed bid, and ask how extra footage, casing, and grouting will be handled if the first target does not produce.

sections.heading: Expected well yield around Mesa
sections.html:
Reported production is reasonably strong in the local records, with a 10.0 gpm median and a middle half from 5.0 to 15.0 gpm. The yield mix shows 43% between 5 and 15 gpm and 37% above 15 gpm. Only 1% report less than 1 gpm, while 19% fall between 1 and 5 gpm.

That is useful for household planning, but a well's pumping rate is not the same as unlimited daily supply. Storage, pump controls, plumbing, and the well's recovery rate matter. Confirm the permit's allowed use before assuming irrigation, livestock, or other demands are covered. Most local permits are domestic or household permits, at 83% of the records.

sections.heading: Mesa water levels and what the record shows
sections.html:
Only 51 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth and permit sample. Where measurements are available, the median depth to water is 73 feet, with the middle half from 30 to 150 feet below the surface.

The decade figures do not show a simple decline in this record. The median measured water level was 100 feet below ground in the 2010s and 68 feet in the 2020s. That difference should not be treated as proof of a rising regional water table because the measured wells and locations may differ. For a purchase, ask for the well construction report, static level, pump test information, and any recent operating problems.

sections.heading: Mesa permit history and active drillers
sections.html:
Well permitting has continued across several decades. The records show 8 permits in the 1950s, 10 in the 1960s, 72 in the 1970s, 79 in the 1980s, 176 in the 1990s, 151 in the 2000s, 57 in the 2010s, and 53 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most common drillers in these records are Rule (Rule, Leo A) with 73 wells, Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) with 71, and Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. (Kissner, Billy D.) with 60. Treat this as permit history, not a current endorsement or guarantee of availability.

sections.heading: What a new Mesa well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground and a drilling rate of $50-$75 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $6,500-$9,800. A finished system, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $12,500-$21,800.

Use that range for early budgeting, not as a guaranteed quote. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, unusual trenching, and electrical distance can change the final price. Ask for a written breakdown separating drilling, casing and completion, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work, testing, and any permit-related work. On a vacant parcel, include driveway and equipment access in the site budget.

sections.heading: Mesa risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
The records show 28 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, along with 3 historic mine features. There are 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set. These facts do not establish contamination at a specific property. Test the well water for ordinary household concerns and contaminants relevant to the parcel's location, and review any available environmental records before closing.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where the area median is favorable. Confirm the well's construction, pump test, static level, and production history. Also verify setbacks and placement for the septic system, replacement area, house, driveway, and drainage. Colorado DWR permit conditions control use; an exempt household-use well is not automatically permission for every proposed use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Mesa, Colorado?
faq.a: Permitted wells within 5 miles of Mesa have a median reported depth of 130 feet. The middle half runs from 80 to 245 feet, and the 90th percentile is 351 feet. About 34% are under 100 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 733 feet. Fractured-bedrock conditions can make one lot differ from its neighbors.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Mesa, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500-$9,800. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $12,500-$21,800. Access, added depth, casing, grouting, and site layout can change a contractor's quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Mesa?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median yield of 10.0 gpm, with the middle half between 5.0 and 15.0 gpm. About 43% produce 5-15 gpm and 37% report more than 15 gpm. Only 1% report under 1 gpm. A pumping rate still needs to be evaluated with storage, recovery, and permitted use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Mesa, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not prove that any individual well is safe or unsafe to drink. There are 28 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so location-specific testing is sensible. Have the water tested before purchase or occupancy, review the construction record, and retest after major well or plumbing work.

faq.q: Are Mesa well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available water-level data do not show a simple decline. The median measured depth to water was 100 feet below ground in the 2010s and 68 feet in the 2020s. Only 51 wells report a static water level, so the samples may not be directly comparable. Check the specific well's static level and pumping history.
